_note: One entry of each shape. See _SCHEMA.md.

copper_ore_kg.basis: per tonne of run-of-mine sulphide ore at the pit head
copper_ore_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED, so there are no material inputs and no cost of production - only labour, and a rent on the deposit set by the poorest ore still worth hauling. The labour figure is the physical work of breaking and moving rock: an ancient miner with hammer, gad and fire-setting moves on the order of 50-60 kg of hard rock per hour in a worked adit, so a tonne is roughly 18 hours. Grade is NOT in this number - it belongs to the smelting entry that consumes this ore, because the same tonne of rock costs the same to dig whether it assays 2% or 4%.

capital.good: copper smelting shaft furnace (clay and stone)
capital.capital_basis: A small ancient/medieval copper shaft furnace is a clay-lined stone stack a couple of metres tall - far smaller than an iron blast furnace because copper melts and reduces at a much lower temperature and campaign scale. Clay and stone quantities are an order-of-magnitude estimate for a structure that size, not a survey of a specific excavated furnace. Service life is set by how long the clay lining survives repeated firing to smelting heat before it cracks and must be relaid - years rather than decades, because unlike a blast furnace's masonry stack there is no separate structural shell outlasting the lining; taken at 6 years as a single blended figure for that reason. Annual output assumes the furnace campaigns for a large fraction of the working year at the batch scale implied by copper_kg's own recipe.

copper_kg.yield_basis: SMELTED, so the yield is grade times recovery. Cyprus and Rio Tinto sulphide ores run 2-4% copper; roast-and-reduction in a shaft furnace recovers on the order of 80% of it, the rest going to slag and flue. One tonne of metal therefore needs 30-60 t of ore, taken here at 50 t. Charcoal is set by the reduction chemistry plus the heat to hold 1200 C through several roasts, about 4 kg per kg of metal, which is why a smelter is sited by a forest rather than by the mine. None of these numbers is derived from the price of copper.

timber_m3.basis: per cubic metre of squared, seasoned construction timber delivered at the wood yard
timber_m3.yield_basis: HARVESTED, so the limit is the forest's annual growth rather than a recipe, and the entry earns a rent on woodland rather than a cost of production. A managed temperate broadleaf woodland puts on roughly 3-5 cubic metres per hectare per year, which is the real constraint on how much timber a region can supply indefinitely. The labour is felling, cross-cutting, hauling and squaring by axe and pit saw; roughly a third of the standing volume is lost to kerf, taper, sapwood and defect, so a cubic metre of usable squared timber starts as about 1.5 standing. Seasoning is time, not labour, and belongs in the build calendar rather than here. LAND (Complaints/49), the worked example of this field's shape (see _SCHEMA.md's WORKED EXAMPLES): unlike the other GROWN entries in this file, timber's own basis is per FINISHED CUBIC METRE, not per hectare-year, so land_iugera_years needs an actual conversion rather than a fixed 1-hectare figure - 1.5 standing m3 (this entry's own felling loss, stated above) / 4 m3/ha/yr mean annual increment (the midpoint of the 3-5 m3/ha/yr this entry already states) = 0.375 ha-years per finished m3, converted to 0.375 / 0.2523 ha/iugerum = 1.4863 iugera-years. Charged against iugerum_land's own solved rent (sim/world/land.py) by sim/solve_prices.py exactly like an ordinary input - see LAND in _SCHEMA.md.
